L14@P0: Abstract
L15@P0: Intracortical brain-computer interfaces (iBCIs) can restore movement and communication abilities to individuals with paralysis by decoding their intended behavior
L16@P0: from neural activity recorded with an implanted device. While this activity yields
L17@P0: high-performance decoding over short timescales, neural data are often nonstationary, which can lead to decoder failure if not accounted for. To maintain performance,
L18@P0: users must frequently recalibrate decoders, which requires the arduous collection of
L19@P0: new neural and behavioral data. Aiming to reduce this burden, several approaches
L20@P0: have been developed that either limit recalibration data requirements (few-shot
L21@P0: approaches) or eliminate explicit recalibration entirely (zero-shot approaches).
L22@P0: However, progress is limited by a lack of standardized datasets and comparison
L23@P0: metrics, causing methods to be compared in an ad hoc manner. Here we introduce the FALCON benchmark suite (Few-shot Algorithms for COnsistent Neural
L24@P0: decoding) to standardize evaluation of iBCI robustness. FALCON curates five
L25@P0: datasets of neural and behavioral data that span movement and communication
L26@P0: tasks to focus on behaviors of interest to modern-day iBCIs. Each dataset includes
L27@P0: calibration data, optional few-shot recalibration data, and private evaluation data.
L28@P0: We implement a flexible evaluation platform which only requires user-submitted
L29@P0: code to return behavioral predictions on unseen data. We also seed the benchmark
L30@P0: by applying baseline methods spanning several classes of possible approaches.
L31@P0: FALCON aims to provide rigorous selection criteria for robust iBCI decoders,
L32@P0: easing their translation to real-world devices. https://snel-repo.github.io/falcon/
L33@P0: 1 Introduction
L34@P0: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) provide a path to restore movement and communication in individuals with paralysis by decoding neuronal population activity to uncover the user’s intention. BCIs
L35@P0: have recently achieved many promising demonstrations, including high degree of freedom robot arm
L36@P0: control [1, 2], computer use and communication [3–8], and speech decoding [9–13]. A specific class
L37@P0: of BCIs known as intracortical BCIs (iBCIs) have enabled many of these impressive technological
L38@P0: feats. However, many of these demonstrations have required decoders to be recalibrated daily or

L42@P1: will require maintaining high performance over long time periods with minimal recalibration. The
L43@P1: challenge here stems from nonstationarities in the neural data that are caused by many factors acting
L44@P1: at multiple timescales, such as shifts in the position of the electrode relative to surrounding tissue,
L45@P1: changes in tissue properties in response to electrode implantation, electrode malfunction, or neural
L46@P1: plasticity [14, 15]. These nonstationarities result in a changing relationship between neural data and
L47@P1: behavior, necessitating frequent decoder recalibration to maintain high performance.
L48@P1: Fortunately, despite these nonstationarities, there are many potential ways to leverage structure in
L49@P1: neural or behavioral data to help reduce the burden of recalibration [16]. For example, while the
L50@P1: spiking activity recorded on an individual iBCI electrode can change over timescales of hours, neural
L51@P1: population activity contains low dimensional structure (manifolds) that shows a consistent relationship
L52@P1: with behavior over months to years [17–19]. Realignment methods that exploit these conserved
L53@P1: manifolds [20–26]can restore decoding without explicit calibration periods. Alternatively, rather

L384@P8: Given FALCON’s flexibility to accommodate many classes of approaches, a method’s held-in score
L385@P8: may be used to contextualize its own held-out score. Oracle decoders establish the approximate
L386@P8: variability in performance between held-in and held-out splits, which appears relatively small (e.g.,
L387@P8: max difference = 0.04 R2for NDT2 Multi on H1, 0.04 WER for RNN Multi on H2). Yet, all methods
L388@P8: show sizable gaps between held-in and held-out scores, far exceeding the expected variability. In
L389@P8: absolute terms, all decoders perform well on held-in M1 (R2 = 0.46-0.78), but performance drops
L390@P8: by 0.12-0.18 R2 on the held-out split (and the RNN has an extreme failure). M2 and H1, which show
L391@P8: lower overall decoding performance, maintain that held-out scores are only a fraction of the potential
L392@P8: performance indicated by held-in scores. This is also true for H2, where CORP provides a great
L393@P8: advance over zero-shot methods but yields error on the held-out datasets that is nearly 4x higher
L394@P8: than that of oracle decoders on average (0.03 vs 0.11 WER). These results indicate that room for
L395@P8: improvement remains in the few-shot challenge on FALCON datasets.
